title: Noel Tata Charts Tata Trusts' New Roadmap Focused on Healthcare and Education
excerpt: Nearly two years after succeeding Ratan Tata, the Tata Trusts chairman is sharpening the philanthropic body's focus on healthcare and education, with spending set to rise to ₹2,000 crore in FY27.
body:
• Tata Trusts under Noel Tata is sharpening its philanthropic roadmap around healthcare and education, with spending set to rise from ₹1,600 crore in FY26 to ₹2,000 crore in FY27.
  • The Trusts' healthcare push spans cancer care networks across five states and a Rs 500 crore investment in the Tata IISc Medical School in Bengaluru.
  • Noel Tata has opposed a public listing of Tata Sons, arguing it would undermine the patient-capital model that funds the Trusts' social mission.
  • Tata Trusts holds a 66% stake in Tata Sons and channels most of its dividend income into philanthropy, a model dating back to the 1890s.

Noel Tata, who took the helm of Tata Trusts in October 2024 after the death of his half-brother Ratan Tata, is charting a sharper roadmap for India's largest philanthropic organisation, centring its next phase of work squarely on healthcare and education. The direction builds on Tata Trusts' legacy but signals a more deliberate channelling of resources toward these two sectors at a time of internal governance debates and rising philanthropic budgets.

Scaling Up Philanthropic Spending

Tata Trusts spent ₹1,600 crore on philanthropic activities in FY26 and plans to scale that to ₹2,000 crore in FY27, according to Tata Trusts CEO Siddharth Sharma. Speaking on LinkedIn in June, Sharma pushed back against media narratives about "chaos" within the Tata group, emphasising the Trusts' core mission.

"The Tata Trusts are continuing to do what they do best — serving those at the margins of society. No hype, no publicity; only solid, hard work. Everything else is noise."

— Siddharth Sharma, CEO, Tata Trusts

The Trusts deploy dividends received from their 66% stake in Tata Sons — the holding company of the $180 billion Tata Group — into charitable causes. In FY24, that dividend totalled Rs 1,712 crore, according to reports from The Hindu BusinessLine.

Healthcare: From Cancer Care to Medical Education

Healthcare has emerged as the centrepiece of Noel Tata's roadmap. The Trusts operate a distributed cancer care network through the Tata Cancer Care Foundation, providing affordable treatment across Assam, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh. The model integrates apex hospitals with smaller step-down centres connected through a hub-and-spoke system, with fellowship programmes training oncologists and pathologists for underserved regions.

Beyond cancer, the Trusts fund programmes targeting non-communicable diseases, mental health, elder care, and maternal healthcare. Their Health Systems Transformation Platform works with state governments to redesign primary care delivery, and a partnership with the central government and Dell is developing a technology platform for nationwide NCD prevention and screening.

In medical education, the Tata Group committed Rs 500 crore to establish the Tata IISc Medical School on the Indian Institute of Science campus in Bengaluru. The school, which began admissions in 2026, offers integrated MD-PhD programmes aimed at creating a new cadre of physician-scientists trained simultaneously in clinical practice and cutting-edge research in areas including oncology, cardiology, and public health.

Education: Deepening Access and Quality

On the education front, Tata Trusts continues to scale programmes that combine technology with grassroots reach. Its partnership with Khan Academy is building localised digital learning resources for middle- and low-income students in India, while the JN Tata Endowment — established in 1892 by Jamsetji Tata — has supported over 5,700 students pursuing higher education abroad. Teacher training initiatives such as the Centre for Excellence in Teacher Education and community mobilisation programmes to bring children back to school round out the portfolio.

Protecting the Philanthropic Model

Noel Tata's roadmap is undergirded by a broader fight to protect the financial architecture that makes it possible. In a letter to the Reserve Bank of India earlier this year, he argued against a proposed public listing of Tata Sons, warning that the move could jeopardise the group's long-standing model of patient capital and philanthropic alignment, according to Moneycontrol. The Trusts fear that public market pressures would prioritise short-term returns over strategic investments in sectors like aviation, semiconductors, and social development.

The listing debate has exposed fissures among Tata Trusts' own trustees, with some members — including Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh — reportedly backing a listing. Noel Tata voted against their reappointment to the board of the Tata Education and Development Trust, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the Tata name carries outsize weight — a symbol of ethical capitalism and nation-building that resonates across borders. Tata Trusts' expanded focus on healthcare and education reinforces that identity. The JN Tata Endowment, which has sent generations of Indian scholars abroad, remains a direct touchpoint for NRIs, and the Trusts' healthcare investments in underserved regions address concerns that many diaspora members share about the state of public services in their home states.

What's Next

The months ahead will test whether Noel Tata can resolve internal governance disputes while scaling the Trusts' philanthropic ambitions. The RBI's decision on Tata Sons' listing status could reshape the funding pipeline entirely. For now, the direction is set: healthcare and education as the twin pillars of a philanthropy that traces its origins back more than 130 years to Jamsetji Tata's founding vision.
nri_angle: Tata Trusts' expanded healthcare and education mandate reinforces the Tata brand's philanthropic identity that overseas Indians closely associate with, while creating potential avenues for diaspora-backed giving and engagement.
